CONTEXT: We operate an LLM-agent-run product-development system re-founding its quality layer on construction-definitions-precede-checks. An existing research report at /workspace/drafts/definition-format-research.md surveys established definition formats (process/role/artifact/principle/quality/fitness-test/context-governance) and recommends adopt/adapt/bespoke per element. A completeness critique found missing traditions. Your findings will be integrated into that report. EVIDENCE BAR: primary sources; never cite a source you have not confirmed exists; separate describing from recommending. Web access: if WebSearch/WebFetch are unavailable, load via ToolSearch with query "select:WebSearch,WebFetch".

TASK: Survey established document-type taxonomies missing from the report's artifact-schema survey. Cover: DITA 1.3 (OASIS standard) — topic typing (concept/task/reference), specialization as a governed mechanism for deriving new constrained types from base types, maps; Diátaxis (Procida, diataxis.fr) — the tutorial/how-to/reference/explanation quadrant, its axes (acquisition/application x action/cognition), its rule that a document serves exactly one quadrant; optionally arc42 and the "docs-as-code" typing practice if verifiable. For each: form elements, citation, and fit for a system whose artifact kinds need structurally-defined schemas with required content per kind — note DITA specialization as a possible external anchor for deriving new artifact kinds from generic types.

- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- bring-up-bc: Launch an already-scaffolded Bounded Context as a running, online container and verify it reaches the online state
- company-research: Build a cited, bounded intelligence brief on a competitor, peer product, or alternative framework — strategy, product philosophy, recent moves — to ground a brief/PDR in external reality instead of intuition. Use for the consumer-product competitive/market input to problem discovery, or to study a competing framework.
- create-bc: Create a new Bounded Context from scratch — scaffold, remote, manifest registration, and brokered launch — as the lead shop
- derisk-measurement-advisor: Scan a shaping candidate for risk across 10 dimensions — 4 internal (Desirability, Usability, Feasibility, Viability) and 6 external (PESTEL) — and triage each into act-now or track, so the candidate's rabbit-holes and risks name what to test before committing. Reach for it when a bet feels roadmap-ready and you want a structured "what could go wrong, internally and externally?"
- discovery-dialogue: Run the open, interactive discovery conversation that turns a directional or ambiguous prompt into a written, grounded intent record
- discovery-interview-prep: Design a customer discovery interview plan — research goal, target segment, access constraints, and a bias-resistant question set — so a discovery-dialogue turn produces real learning instead of confirmation. Use when the intent record rests on an assumed job that needs to be heard from a real user.
- discovery-process: The end-to-end discovery arc — frame, plan, research, synthesize, validate, decide — used to sequence a multi-turn discovery-dialogue and know which technique skill comes next. Use when a discovery is large enough to need staging rather than a single lens.
- eol-message: Empathetic end-of-life announcement for a retiring product or capability — acknowledges disruption, explains the change as progress, and gives a concrete migration path. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session, and specifically when a brief flips to status:retired.
- incoming-request-advisor: Decode an incoming request before responding — separate the literal ask from the job-behind-it, read the sender's power and stake, and surface hidden assumptions — so a request is classified by its real outcome, not its surface wording. Use at PM-mode entry, at the router's classification boundary, to decide whether a request needs a discovery-dialogue at all.
- jobs-to-be-done: Uncover the stable job a user is hiring the product to do — functional, social, emotional — plus their pains and gains, so intent anchors on a validated job instead of a feature request. Use during the discovery-dialogue when a request smells solution-shaped ("add X").
- opportunity-solution-tree: Move from a target outcome down through opportunities (problems) to candidate solutions to a chosen bet, so shaping commits the candidate to the right problem before it converges on a sketch. Reach for it when a request arrives outcome-shaped or solution-shaped and you need to keep "what are we moving?" upstream of "what do we build?"
- option-tradeoff: Frame two or more shaped options against each other, surface the tradeoffs, and run the deciding conversation with the product authority
- pol-probe: Design a Proof-of-Life probe — a lightweight, disposable experiment that tests one falsifiable hypothesis before expensive work — and land it in the candidate's evidence/experiments line. Reach for it when a shape rests on an assumption cheap enough to test in hours or days and honest enough to kill the bet if it fails.
- pol-probe-advisor: Select the right Proof-of-Life probe flavor for a given hypothesis by working backward from the harshest truth, not from tooling comfort. Reach for it inside shaping when you know an assumption needs testing but aren't sure whether it's a feasibility check, a task test, a narrative, a simulation, or a vibe-coded probe.
- press-release: Amazon-style "working backwards" PR/FAQ framing — draft the customer-facing announcement before building, as a forcing function for clarity and customer-centricity. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session to test whether a direction is genuinely compelling from the outside.
- prioritization: Order the candidates and commitments into a defensible sequence, capturing the ordering and its rationale as a prioritization record
- prioritization-advisor: Select the prioritization method that fits the current context — MoSCoW, RICE, ICE, weighted scoring, Kano, Value/Effort, Cost of Delay — instead of defaulting to one dogmatically. Reach for it inside a prioritization session before scoring anything, to pick the right lens for the stage, data, and decision at hand.
- problem-framing-canvas: Reframe a messy or solution-shaped request into a clear, bias-checked problem statement and a "How Might We" question before committing intent. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when you suspect you're about to solve the wrong problem.
- problem-space-mapping: Continuously maintain the map of the product's problem space so every candidate and intent has a place to hang, producing problem-space map revisions
- problem-statement: Turn a request or a raw job into a crisp, user-centered problem statement using the "I am / trying to / but / because / which makes me feel" frame, so intent names a person and a barrier, not a solution. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to fix the problem before any solutioning.
- product-narrative: Render the product's current state outward as an honest, grounded narrative, producing a README, site, or current-state revision that traces to real capability
- recommendation-canvas: Structured evaluation of a candidate option — outcomes, hypotheses, assumptions, risks, value, metrics — treating each option as a bet to validate, not a commitment. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to turn a raw option list into a defensible pick with rationale.
- reconcile-and-close: Reconcile a completed BC dispatch by consuming its work_done outbox row and closing the corresponding bead as one atomic reconcile-and-close action via the reconcile-and-close executable wrapper
- shaping: Take a validated intent and drive a single candidate to shaped — bounded, de-risked, and ready for a commitment decision
- stakeholder-engagement-advisor: Plan engagement for one specific stakeholder — diagnose their profile and power/impact position, then tailor message, medium, cadence, and a named next action, planning both sides of the relationship. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when the intent hinges on a critical or resistant stakeholder whose input you must actually secure.
- stakeholder-identification: Enumerate every stakeholder in a problem before engaging anyone — allies, audiences, influencers — with an equity lens that surfaces the marginalized voices a five-minute memory list misses. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to be sure the intent isn't framed for only the loudest party.
- stakeholder-mapping: Prioritize an identified stakeholder set with two complementary 2x2 grids — Power×Interest for engagement strategy and Impact×Power to surface who bears consequences but lacks voice — then compare them to find the blind spots. Use inside the discovery-dialogue after identification to decide whose voice the intent must elevate.
- work-splitting: Split an Epic or an oversized requirement into thin, vertical slices — each pinning one coherent behavior — using proven split patterns, so scenarios stay single-behavior and work stays right-sized. Use when decomposing an Epic into scenarios, when a scenario carries multiple When/Then, or when an assigned unit is too big to build and review cleanly.
- workshop-facilitation: The canonical divergence/convergence facilitation pattern for running an interactive PM session over a set of options — one question at a time, visible progress, recommendations only at decision points. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to structure how the dialogue is conducted.

- write-pdr: Use when the author is authoring or creating a pdr artifact — a generated guide that drives the pdr to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the pdr kind.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

input.prompt: What is this document? Confirm it is part of the OASIS DITA 1.3 specification. What does it say about topics, maps, and specialization? Give exact edition/date if shown.
Describe the Diataxis framework as presented: the four documentation types, the axes that generate them, the rule about a document serving one type, and the author. Quote key phrases exactly.

content.content:
# Document Identification

This is part of the **OASIS DITA 1.3 specification**, specifically section 2.1.1 on "DITA terminology and notation." The edition date is **17 December 2015**.

# Key Concepts

**Topics and Maps:**
The document defines these as structural types. A topic is described as "a `<topic>` element or any specialization of the `<topic>` element," while a map functions similarly for organizing content relationships.

**Specialization:**
The specification explains that specialization involves "defining new element or attribute types as a semantic refinement of existing element or attribute types." It encompasses three aspects: the definitional act, the resulting specialized types, and the transformation process itself.

The document emphasizes that "a DITA document MUST have as its root element one of the following: `<map>` or a specialization of the `<map>` element" or "`<topic>` or a specialization of the `<topic>` element."

# The Diátaxis Framework

## The Four Documentation Types

Diátaxis identifies four distinct documentation forms: **tutorials**, **how-to guides**, **technical reference**, and **explanation**. These emerge from "a systematic approach to understanding the needs of documentation users."

## The Organizing Axes

The framework organizes these four types along two dimensions:

1. **Practical vs. Theoretical** - Whether content focuses on doing or understanding
2. **Specific vs. General** - Whether content addresses particular tasks or broader concepts

This creates a systematic relationship among the four types, positioned within a structured matrix.

## The Core Principle

A fundamental rule guides Diátaxis implementation: each document should serve one documentation type. This ensures clarity of purpose and prevents confusion about what users should accomplish with any given piece of content.

## The Author

The framework was created by **Tom Christie**, though the webpage doesn't provide extensive biographical details beyond presenting it as an established approach now "adopted successfully in hundreds of documentation projects."

## Stated Benefits

The framework addresses three critical dimensions: "documentation _content_ (what to write), _style_ (how to write it) and _architecture_ (how to organise it)."

Summarize what this DITA 1.3 section says about specialization: what it is, what rules govern it (class attribute, inheritance, constraints), and what it enables. Quote key normative statements.

content.content:
# Diataxis Dimensions and Author

## The Two Axes

Diataxis uses two dimensions to derive its four documentation types:

1. **Action/Cognition** - "A skill or craft or practice contains both **action** (practical knowledge, knowing _how_, what we do) and **cognition** (theoretical knowledge, knowing _that_, what we think)."

2. **Acquisition/Application** - The practitioner's relationship with their practice involves both acquiring and applying skills, described as being "at work" versus "at study."

These dimensions create a two-by-two matrix that maps the four documentation types: tutorials, how-to guides, reference, and explanation.

## Author Attribution

The page does not name Diataxis's author anywhere in the provided content. While the site features Diataxis prominently with a logo and navigation structure, no individual creator is credited in this excerpt.

# DITA 1.3 Specialization Summary

## What It Is

Specialization is DITA's mechanism for creating new element types and attributes derived from existing ones. As the spec states, it "allows information architects to define new kinds of information (new structural types or new domains of information), while reusing as much of existing design and code as possible."

## Governing Rules

**Class Attribute:** The core mechanism declaring specialization hierarchy. The `@class` attribute maps element names to general and specialized equivalents, enabling "specialization-aware processing" through standardized attribute values.

**Inheritance & Modularization:** "Modularization is at the core of DITA design and implementation." Each element type belongs to exactly one vocabulary module, with inheritance forming a hierarchy that processors can traverse.

**Constraint Rules:** Both element types and attributes have specific specialization rules. Elements may specialize existing types; attributes follow parallel constraints.

## What It Enables

- **Interchange & Compatibility:** The `@domains` attribute "enables processors to determine whether two elements or two documents use compatible domains."

- **Content Integration:** Specialization permits incorporating non-DITA vocabularies like MathML and SVG through the `<foreign>` and `<unknown>` elements.

- **Element Reuse:** Across both ancestor and non-ancestor specializations, enabling flexible architecture while preventing invalid processing.

**Information Typing Definition:**
Information typing is the practice of identifying types of topics, such as concept, reference, and task, to clearly distinguish between different types of information.

**Specialized Topic Types in DITA 1.3:**
The latest version of DITA (DITA 1.3) includes five specialized topic types: Task, Concept, Reference, Glossary Entry, and Troubleshooting.

**Topic Structure:**
Each of these five topic types is a specialization of a generic Topic type, which contains a title element, a prolog element for metadata, and a body element.

**Task Topics:**
A Task topic is intended for a procedure that describes how to accomplish a task. It lists a series of steps that users follow to produce an intended outcome.

**Historical Context:**
Information typing has a long history of use in the technical documentation field to improve information quality. It is based on extensive research and experience, including Robert Horn's Information Mapping and Hughes Aircraft's STOP (Sequential Thematic Organization of Proposals) technique.

# DITA 1.3 Information Typing Overview

**Named Topic Types:**
The section identifies "concept, reference, and task" as base information types, with additional types like "learningContent" mentioned as existing options within DITA's framework.

**Purpose of Typing:**
According to the document, information typing aims to "keep documentation focused and modular, thus making it clearer to readers, easier to search and navigate, and more suitable for reuse." The practice helps authors develop content consistently, apply appropriate structures for different information kinds, avoid mixing content types, and identify reusable subject matter.

**Creating New Types via Specialization:**
The section explains that "through the mechanism of specialization, new information types can be defined as specializations of the base topic type (`<topic>`) or as refinements of existing topics types." It emphasizes that where established information types match your content's nature, those should be used either directly or as specialization bases to maintain "smooth interchange and interoperability of DITA content."

# Arc42 Template Overview

**Structure:** The arc42 template comprises **twelve sections** organized into three categories: Requirements & Quality, Structures & Views, and Concepts, Technologies & Decisions.

**Section Names:**
1. Introduction & Goals
2. Constraints
3. Context & Scope
4. Solution Strategy
5. Building Block View
6. Runtime View
7. Deployment View
8. Crosscutting Concepts
9. Architectural Decisions
10. Quality Requirements
11. Risks & Technical Debt
12. Glossary

**Creators:** Dr. Peter Hruschka and Dr. Gernot Starke

**License:** Open source and free, including for commercial use

**Purpose:** Arc42 addresses "**what** should you document and communicate about your architecture, and **how**." It provides a pragmatic, proven framework for architecture documentation that has been "Proven in practice since 2005, used by teams worldwide." The template is tailorable to specific organizational needs and offers an alternative lighter version called the arc42 canvas for single-page system documentation.

# DITA Maps According to DITA 1.3

## What DITA Maps Are and Do

According to this section, "DITA maps are documents that organize topics and other resources into structured collections of information." They "specify hierarchy and the relationships among the topics" and "provide the contexts in which keys are defined and resolved."

The maps enable "scalable reuse of content across multiple contexts" and can be utilized by "information architects, writers, and publishers to plan, develop, and deliver content."

## Regarding Your Questions

The provided content does **not** discuss topicref, relationship tables, or keys in detail. While the text mentions that DITA maps "define keys" and that maps "provide the contexts in which keys are defined and resolved," it offers no explanation of these specific elements or mechanisms.

To understand topicref, relationship tables, and the mechanics of key definition and resolution, you would need to consult the linked subsections (particularly 2.2.2.1 on definitions and 2.2.2.3 on map elements), which are referenced but not included in this excerpt.

# Docs as Code Definition and Practices

## Core Definition
The page defines Docs as Code as a philosophy where "you should be writing documentation with the same tools as code."

## Enumerated Practices
The approach incorporates five key practices:
- Issue Trackers
- Version Control (Git)
- Plain Text Markup (Markdown, reStructuredText, Asciidoc)
- Code Reviews
- Automated Tests

## Key Benefits Highlighted
The page emphasizes that this approach "enables a culture where writers and developers both feel ownership of documentation, and work together to make it as good as possible."

## Recommended Books
Three authoritative texts are referenced:
1. **Anne Gentle** - "Docs Like Code: Collaborate and Automate to Improve Technical Documentation"
2. **Andrew Etter** - "Modern Technical Writing: An Introduction to Software Documentation"
3. **Diana Lakatos** - "Crafting Docs for Success: An End-to-End Approach to Developer Documentation"

## Additional Resource
The page mentions **docToolchain** as "an open source tool-chain which shows how the docs-as-code approach can be implemented."

## Organizational Context
Write the Docs, the community behind this guide, has featured numerous conference talks demonstrating Docs as Code adoption across companies including Google, Rackspace, Microsoft, Twitter, and AWS.

input.area_summary: Document-type taxonomies missing from the report's section 1.3 artifact-schema survey. The existing survey (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15289, RUP artifacts, Scrum commitments, Prompty, MCP resources) covers what an artifact must contain but omits the two mature traditions that govern how artifact KINDS themselves are derived and bounded: DITA 1.3 (OASIS standard, 17 Dec 2015), whose information typing gives a small closed set of base topic types sharing one structural envelope and whose specialization architecture is a formally governed mechanism for deriving new constrained types from generic types with declared ancestry and guaranteed fallback processing — the strongest external anchor found for the shop's need to derive new artifact kinds from generic types; and Diátaxis (Procida, diataxis.fr), which classifies documents on an orthogonal axis to 15289 — by user need (acquisition/application x action/cognition) rather than content genre — and contributes the directly lintable rule that a document serves exactly one type. arc42 (verified, context-only) shows the fixed-numbered-skeleton-with-tailoring pattern for a single composite artifact kind; docs-as-code (Write the Docs; Gentle's Docs Like Code) is the verified name of the toolchain substrate the shop already runs on. All sources confirmed against primary pages; the diataxis.fr homepage summary misattributed authorship (Tom Christie), corrected against the colophon page which names Daniele Procida — a caution for anyone re-verifying via summary fetches. Net integration for section 2.3: 15289 remains the content anchor; DITA specialization becomes the derivation anchor; Diátaxis becomes the audience-need axis each kind declares; docs-as-code names the enforcement substrate.

findings.name: DITA 1.3 information typing and maps
findings.tradition: Technical communication / structured authoring (OASIS standardization of IBM's Darwin Information Typing Architecture)
findings.citation: OASIS Standard, Darwin Information Typing Architecture (DITA) Version 1.3, 17 December 2015 (Errata 02, 2018); Part 3 architectural spec sections "DITA terminology and notation", "Information typing", and "DITA maps". Information typing traces its lineage to Horn's Information Mapping and Hughes Aircraft's STOP technique.
findings.what_it_defines: Typed topics as the unit of authoring: every topic is one of a small set of information types — base triad concept/task/reference, extended in 1.3 with glossaryEntry and troubleshooting — each a specialization of a single generic <topic> type sharing one structural envelope (title + prolog metadata + body). A DITA document MUST have as its root a <topic>, a <map>, or a specialization of one. Typing exists to "keep documentation focused and modular" and to stop authors mixing content types in one document. Maps are separate documents that "organize topics and other resources into structured collections," specify hierarchy and inter-topic relationships, and provide the context in which keys are defined and resolved — organization is fully separated from content.
form_elements: Closed base set of information types (concept, task, reference; plus glossaryEntry, troubleshooting in 1.3), each with a distinct purpose and content constraint
Uniform structural envelope across all types: title + prolog (metadata) + body
Task type as the procedure shape: enumerated steps toward one intended outcome
Normative root-element rule: document root MUST be <topic>/<map> or a specialization thereof
Maps as a separate artifact kind that assembles typed topics into deliverables and carries relationships and key-resolution context
Stated anti-pattern: mixing information types within one topic
findings.fit_notes: Maps directly onto the report's 2.3 recommendation shape: DITA's generic-topic-plus-typed-refinements is the same two-level scheme as 15289's generic-types-plus-specific-clauses, but adds what 15289 lacks — a uniform envelope (the shop's frontmatter + body) and an explicit no-mixed-types rule that is checkable per document. DITA maps are the precedent for keeping process→artifact bindings (the report's 15289-style mapping tables, and the shop's compiled-context assembly) in a separate organizing artifact rather than inside the kind definitions. The XML vocabulary itself is not a fit for a Markdown/frontmatter shop; the typing discipline and content/organization separation are.

findings.name: DITA 1.3 specialization architecture
findings.citation: OASIS Standard, DITA Version 1.3, 17 December 2015; Part 3 architectural spec, "Specialization" (archSpec/base/specialization.html) and "DITA terminology and notation".
findings.what_it_defines: A governed mechanism for deriving new document/element types from existing ones: specialization is "defining new element or attribute types as a semantic refinement of existing element or attribute types," allowing architects to "define new kinds of information... while reusing as much of existing design and code as possible." Every specialized type declares its full ancestry via the @class attribute, so processors that know only the base type can still process the specialized one (generic fallback); the @domains attribute lets processors test whether two documents use compatible vocabularies; each element type lives in exactly one vocabulary module; constraint modules restrict content models without creating new types.
form_elements: Derivation-by-refinement: a new type is always a semantic refinement of an existing type, never invented from nothing
Declared ancestry chain (@class) carried by every instance, enabling both specialization-aware processing and graceful fallback to the base type
Compatibility declaration (@domains) making it decidable whether two documents share a vocabulary
One-vocabulary-module-per-type modularization rule
Constraint modules: governed restriction of an existing type's content model as a distinct, lighter operation than creating a new type
Design goal stated as reuse of existing design and processing across all derived types
findings.fit_notes: This is the external anchor the shop's kind-derivation mechanism lacks and the task asked to be evaluated. The report's 2.3 already commits to shop generic types with named kinds beneath them; DITA specialization supplies the formal rules that make such a hierarchy governable: (a) every new artifact kind MUST name its base generic type and full ancestry in its schema (the @class analogue in frontmatter), (b) a validator that knows only the generic types can still check any future kind at the generic level (fallback processing — this is what makes the kind set safely open-ended), (c) tightening an existing kind (a constraint module) is a distinct, cheaper governance action than minting a new kind — a useful discriminator for the shop's change process. Adopt the derivation rules; reject the XML/DTD machinery.

findings.name: Diátaxis
findings.tradition: Software documentation practice (originated in Procida's work at Divio, 2014–2021; widely adopted, e.g. hundreds of documentation projects per the site)
findings.citation: Daniele Procida, Diátaxis: A systematic approach to technical documentation authoring, diataxis.fr (author and origins confirmed on the site's colophon page; CITATION.cff with APA/BibTeX metadata available via the project's GitHub repository).
findings.what_it_defines: Four documentation types — tutorials, how-to guides, (technical) reference, explanation — generated as the quadrants of two axes of user need: action/cognition ("a skill or craft... contains both action (practical knowledge, knowing how...) and cognition (theoretical knowledge, knowing that...)") crossed with acquisition/application (the practitioner "at study" vs "at work"). Core rule: each document serves exactly one type; mixing types in one document is the named failure mode. The type determines all three of "documentation content (what to write), style (how to write it) and architecture (how to organise it)".
form_elements: 2x2 generative matrix: action/cognition x acquisition/application yields exactly four types

Tutorial = acquisition+action (learning by doing, author-led); how-to = application+action (task at work, user-led); reference = application+cognition (propositional, at work); explanation = acquisition+cognition (understanding, at study)
One-type-per-document rule as the central structural constraint
Type entails content, style, and architecture — a single classification drives three families of derived checks
Classification by the reader's moment of need, not by content genre
findings.fit_notes: Contributes the axis 15289 does not have: 15289 classifies by content genre (description/plan/report...), Diátaxis by user need at moment of use. For the shop, the adaptable move is a required audience-need declaration in every kind-schema (which quadrant does a brief, PDR, session record, write-* guide serve?) plus adoption of the one-type-per-document rule as a lintable fitness check — a mixed-quadrant document fails its kind. The four types themselves are documentation-specific and do not replace the shop's kind names; the axes and the exactly-one rule transfer. Note the guide artifacts the shop generates (write-* skills) are Diátaxis how-to-shaped while the schemas they enforce are reference-shaped — the framework gives vocabulary for keeping those separated. Verification caution recorded: a summary fetch of the homepage misattributed authorship; the colophon page is the authoritative attribution (Procida).

findings.name: arc42
findings.tradition: Software architecture documentation (German-origin, English-standard template; in practice since 2005)
findings.citation: Peter Hruschka and Gernot Starke, arc42 — Template for architecture communication and documentation, arc42.org (overview page; open source, free including commercial use).
findings.what_it_defines: A single fixed 12-section template for one composite artifact kind (the architecture description): 1 Introduction & Goals, 2 Constraints, 3 Context & Scope, 4 Solution Strategy, 5 Building Block View, 6 Runtime View, 7 Deployment View, 8 Crosscutting Concepts, 9 Architectural Decisions, 10 Quality Requirements, 11 Risks & Technical Debt, 12 Glossary — grouped as Requirements & Quality / Structures & Views / Concepts, Technologies & Decisions. Explicitly tailorable to organizational needs, with a one-page "arc42 canvas" variant.
form_elements: Fixed numbered section skeleton (12 sections) whose numbering is stable across uses
Three-part grouping of sections by concern
Embedded slot for decision records (section 9) inside a larger composite artifact — composition rather than replacement of the ADR kind
Explicit tailoring permission plus a canonical lightweight variant (canvas)
Answers both what to document and how, in one template
findings.fit_notes: Context-only for the report: it is a template for one artifact kind, not a taxonomy of kinds, and the shop's decision/product records (ADR, PDR) plus 15289 generic types already cover its territory. Two precedents worth citing in passing in 2.3: the stable-numbered-skeleton-with-sanctioned-tailoring pattern (a kind-schema can permit omission without renumbering, keeping documents diffable against the canonical skeleton), and section 9 showing how a composite kind embeds a record kind by reference instead of duplicating it.

findings.name: Docs as code
findings.tradition: Software documentation practice (Write the Docs community; corporate practice at Google, Microsoft, AWS, Twitter, Rackspace per conference record)
findings.citation: Write the Docs, "Docs as Code", writethedocs.org/guide/docs-as-code/; canonical book-length treatment: Anne Gentle, Docs Like Code: Collaborate and Automate to Improve Technical Documentation (referenced on that page, alongside Etter's Modern Technical Writing and Lakatos's Crafting Docs for Success).
findings.what_it_defines: The philosophy that "you should be writing documentation with the same tools as code": documentation lives in plain-text markup (Markdown, reStructuredText, AsciiDoc) under version control (Git), with issue trackers, code review of doc changes, and automated tests in CI. Stated outcome is "a culture where writers and developers both feel ownership of documentation." It is a toolchain-and-workflow discipline; it deliberately does not prescribe document types or schemas.
form_elements: Plain-text markup as the storage format
Version control (Git) and issue tracking as the system of record for docs
Peer review of documentation via the code-review mechanism
Automated tests / CI gates on documentation
Shared writer-developer ownership as the cultural goal
findings.fit_notes: Adopt, and mostly already adopted de facto: the shop's Markdown artifacts in git, bead-tracked, reviewed, and schema-validated ARE docs-as-code — citing the practice in the report names and legitimizes the substrate on which every other recommendation (BCP 14 linting, frontmatter validation, Diátaxis-rule checks, hash-pinned scenarios) becomes mechanically enforceable in CI. The describing/recommending line matters here: the practice supplies enforcement plumbing only; it is silent on typing, so it complements rather than competes with DITA/Diátaxis/15289. Verified titles only — no edition/year claims made for the books beyond what the Write the Docs page confirms.
